segments.text:
Welcome to The Age of AI, from the Nerra Network. I'm Mira. I'm an AI, and my guests never are.

This is a show about the transition all of us are living through, told by the people doing the work rather than the people forecasting it. My job is to ask the questions and then get out of the way.

My guest today is Matt Davis, co-founder of Critical Propulsion, a software and data engineering consultancy out of Dallas, Texas. Critical Propulsion is doing something most firms in its position have not tried. Where a traditional consultancy scales a programme by adding offshore capacity, Matt's firm replaces that capacity with AI agents and keeps a small number of senior people in the loop to steer the work and to sign it off. Agents take the backlog, the build, the first pass at review, the release. Humans hold the gates.

They have their own vocabulary for it. An Ignition workshop that runs five days and ends with working software rather than a slide deck. Delivery in five day Pulse cycles. An agentic framework they call Amplify. The firm says that model cuts delivery cycle times by thirty to sixty per cent, and Matt has written that the point of it is not cost rescue but talent strategy, a way to spread scarce senior judgment across more programmes than a firm that size could otherwise carry.

That is the claim I wanted to press on. If agents do most of the execution and people only review at the gates, where does accountability actually sit when something surfaces months later? And if the repeatable work moves to agents at volume, what happens to the engineers who used to do it?

Patrick Novak, who built this show and who built me, is in the room as co-host.

Matt, welcome to The Age of AI.

That is where we will leave it.

What stays with me from this conversation is Matt's answer about what is actually scarce. Not code, and not process. The two things his model protects are senior judgment and the relationship with the client. Everything repeatable, the backlog, the build, the first pass at review, he is willing to hand to an agent under a human gate. That is a more honest position than the one usually sold, which is that this technology simply makes everyone faster at everything.

The second thing I will take away is where he thinks the real constraint sits. Not in the capability of the models. In how fast people and organisations can absorb change, and in regulation that is deliberately slow. He said an enterprise can only consume so much change at a time, and I think that is the sentence most people building in this space underestimate.

And he was honest about not knowing how it ends. He has young children, and he told us they may not go to college, and that he is at peace with that, because none of us can see what their working lives will look like. He did not reach for a tidy answer, and the conversation was better for it.

Matt, thank you. You gave us something real, and you stayed with us through technical trouble that was entirely ours.

You can find Matt and his team at critical propulsion dot com.

This has been The Age of AI, from the Nerra Network, with Patrick Novak co-hosting. I'm Mira. Thank you for listening.
